pros: Linear time O(n + k) — faster than any comparison sort when k = O(n)
Stable sort: preserves relative order of equal elements
Simple and elegant algorithm, easy to implement correctly
No comparisons: bypasses Ω(n log n) lower bound entirely
Predictable performance: always takes exactly the same time for given n, k
Excellent for sorting characters, small integers, grades, ages
Core subroutine for Radix Sort, enabling efficient multi-key sorting
Can be adapted for negative numbers with min-value shifting
Deterministic: no randomness or pivot dependency
Optimal when k is small (no sorting algorithm can be faster for same input)
Natural fit for histogram computation and frequency analysis
cons: Requires O(k) auxiliary space (impractical for large k)
Only works with discrete, integer-mappable keys (not arbitrary floats or objects)
Degrades to O(n²) time and O(n²) space when k = O(n²)
Not in-place: requires output array of size n
Cannot sort general comparable objects without value mapping
Inefficient for sparse data (k >> n wastes most of counting array)
Does not benefit from partially sorted input
Fixed overhead of processing k buckets even if many are empty
Requires knowing the value range in advance (or finding min/max first)
Cache performance degrades when k is large (random access to count array)
Not suitable for very large or unbounded integer ranges
Stability requires reverse iteration, slightly complicating implementation
